c1:p0: This opening passage introduces the novel's protagonist, Lucilla Marjoribanks, and the death of her mother that sets the entire plot in motion. c1:p1: This chunk appears immediately after Miss Marjoribanks loses her mother at age fifteen while away at school. c1:p2: This passage describes Mrs. Marjoribanks's response to being neglected and undervalued as an invalid during her final years. c6:p35: Lucilla asks her father how long it has been since he married, prompting reflection on his marriage to her late mother. c6:p37: Lucilla persuades her father to refurnish the drawing-room by arguing that the room's color should complement her complexion, just as dress colors do. c6:p38: Lucilla decides to refurnish the drawing room with a pale spring green color that will complement her complexion, part of her plan to organize the household and prepare for hosting "Evenings" for society.
c6:p39: Lucilla has just announced her intention to refurnish the drawing-room with a color scheme suited to her complexion. c6:p40: Dr Marjoribanks is amused by his daughter Lucilla's clever boldness in examining her complexion in the mirror to determine what color drawing-room furniture would suit her best. c6:p41: Dr. Marjoribanks observes his daughter Lucilla examining her complexion in the mirror to determine what color drawing-room carpet would suit her best. c6:p42: Lucilla negotiates with her father to refurnish the drawing-room, arguing that the color scheme should complement her complexion. c6:p43: Lucilla argues to her father for refurnishing the drawing-room, explaining that while clothing can be changed frequently, furniture is permanent. c6:p44: Lucilla is persuading her father to refurnish the drawing-room by arguing for a pale spring green color scheme that would complement her complexion. c6:p45: The Doctor questions Lucilla about her assumption that he intends to refurnish the drawing room, revealing his conflicted feelings—irritated by her presumption but secretly delighted by her cleverness and confidence in managing household matters.
c6:p46: Dr. Marjoribanks questions Lucilla's assumption that he will refurnish the drawing-room, skeptically asking what he will do with the expensive furniture when she eventually marries and leaves him alone in the house.
c6:p47: Tom inopportunely interrupts a conversation between Lucilla and her father about whether she will marry and leave the house. c6:p48: Lucilla responds to her father's concern about refurnishing the drawing-room, arguing that she plans to remain at home for ten years before potentially marrying. c6:p49: Lucilla responds to her father's concern about refurnishing the drawing-room by claiming she will remain unmarried for ten years to enjoy the improvements, then asks Tom to re-measure the room's length while she calculates carpet requirements for the new green color scheme she has chosen.
c6:p50: Tom has been measuring the drawing room at Lucilla's insistence to determine carpet dimensions. c6:p51: Tom has arrived unexpectedly at the Doctor's house and is being entertained by Lucilla in the drawing-room. c6:p52: The Doctor observes Tom measuring the drawing room at Lucilla's request and realizes he disapproves of his nephew courting his daughter, despite having just complained to Providence about not having a son.
c6:p53: The Doctor observes Tom Marjoribanks paying attention to Lucilla and realizes Tom could serve as the son he previously wished for, yet he is dismayed by this prospect because Tom has no prospects and the Doctor disdains the idea of his accomplished daughter marrying a man of no fortune.
c6:p54: The Doctor, initially wishing for a son instead of his daughter Lucilla, becomes concerned when he realizes Tom Marjoribanks is paying romantic attention to her. c6:p55: Dr. Marjoribanks decides to remain in the drawing-room despite his boredom, observing his daughter Lucilla and his nephew Tom as Lucilla directs Tom to measure the room for new carpets. c6:p56: Tom has arrived unexpectedly for a visit, and after supper, Lucilla begins discussing plans to refurnish the drawing-room in pale spring green to suit her complexion. This description captures Lucilla's appearance as she stands by the fire during the measuring discussion, noting how her green ribbons complement her coloring and how she manages to carry off the fashionable but challenging pale green color despite her substantial figure.
c6:p57: Lucilla is supervising Tom's measurement of the drawing-room to determine carpet requirements. She criticizes his striding gait and insists he take moderate steps, claiming she was managing the task perfectly well before his arrival interrupted her.
c6:p58: Lucilla is directing Tom to measure the drawing-room by pacing its length to determine how much carpet is needed. c6:p59: Tom is measuring the drawing-room's dimensions by pacing it out at Lucilla's request to determine carpet requirements. c6:p60: Dr. Marjoribanks interrupts Tom's room-measuring task and offers to provide the room's dimensions himself. He assumes Lucilla wants to host parties with dancing and singing, and disapproves, insisting she must wait until marriage for such entertainments.
c6:p61: Lucilla responds to her father's concern about her entertaining plans by reassuring him that she intends to host refined "Evenings" rather than frivolous parties with dancing, positioning herself as devoted to his comfort while introducing her vision for transforming the household's social role.
c6:p62: Lucilla manages her father and cousin Tom by dismissing her father for the evening while graciously offering to keep the tired Tom company, thereby demonstrating her domestic devotion while subtly asserting control over the household and its inhabitants.
c6:p63: Lucilla has just announced her intention to host "Evenings" rather than dances to entertain society and be a comfort to her father. c6:p64: Tom Marjoribanks has arrived unexpectedly at his uncle the Doctor's house. # Context

After Tom Marjoribanks arrives unexpectedly at the Doctor's house, Lucilla establishes her intention to have "Evenings" (social gatherings) in the refurnished drawing-room rather than engage in dancing and parties. When the Doctor and Tom leave the drawing-room, the Doctor reflects on Lucilla's clever handling of Tom and her refined social aspirations, finding himself charmed by her intelligence and considering refurnishing the room to complement her complexion.
c6:p66: The Doctor, after Lucilla announces her intention to host "Evenings" rather than parties in the drawing-room, retreats to his library. Reflecting on his daughter's cleverness in managing Tom and her superior attitude toward vulgar festivities, he becomes amused by her scheme to refurnish the drawing-room to suit her complexion. c7:p0: This is the opening paragraph of the chapter. The paragraph sets up the tension between Lucilla's important plans and Tom's desire to spend time with her.
c7:p1: Lucilla Marjoribanks begins her day with plans for her father's first dinner party under her new management. She decides to invite Mrs. Chiley as a chaperone, marking the beginning of her systematic reorganization of her father's household and social life to become indispensable to him.
c7:p2: Lucilla is planning her father's first dinner party under her new management. c7:p4: Lucilla is explaining to her father, Dr. Marjoribanks, why she needs Mrs. Chiley to serve as her chaperone for his dinner party that evening. c7:p5: Dr. Marjoribanks reacts with amusement mixed with resignation upon learning that his daughter Lucilla intends to invite Mrs. Chiley as a chaperone for his dinner party that evening, recognizing this as the beginning of the domestic changes he fears—the entrance of the "female element" that will transform the character of his household and his dinner parties.

c7:p7: Dr. Marjoribanks reluctantly agrees to have Mrs. Chiley as a chaperone for his daughter Lucilla at his dinner party that evening, though he is displeased about it because it means Mrs. Chiley will sit at his right hand as the senior female guest, disrupting his usual enjoyment of hosting dinners. c7:p8: The Doctor has reluctantly agreed to have Mrs Chiley attend his dinner party as a chaperone for Lucilla, though he is displeased at the prospect of her sitting at his right hand as hostess. c7:p9: The Doctor reluctantly agrees to have Mrs. Chiley attend his dinner party as a chaperone for his daughter Lucilla, despite his displeasure at the arrangement. c7:p10: The Doctor begins to realize the consequences of allowing his daughter Lucilla to take charge of household management. c7:p11: Lucilla dismisses her cousin Tom from her morning, instructing him to leave and only return at luncheon if he brings someone amusing to entertain her guests. c7:p12: Lucilla dismisses her cousin Tom from the house in the morning, instructing him that he may return for lunch only if he brings someone amusing to entertain her and any visiting friends. c7:p13: Lucilla dismisses her cousin Tom from the house, instructing him to return only at luncheon if he brings someone amusing. c7:p14: Tom Marjoribanks misunderstands Lucilla's stated life purpose of being a comfort to her father, failing to recognize that her filial devotion is genuine and that she truly intends to remain unmarried until age twenty-nine, dismissing her claims as mere social pretense rather than sincere conviction.
c7:p15: Tom Marjoribanks, Lucilla's cousin, has just been dismissed from her company with instructions to either stay away or return at half-past one with someone amusing. c7:p17: After dismissing her cousin Tom from the house, Lucilla visits Mrs Chiley to invite her as a chaperone for her father's dinner party that evening—the first formal dinner under Lucilla's new management of the household. c7:p18: Mrs Chiley expresses her enthusiasm about attending Dr Marjoribanks's dinner party that evening and seeks Lucilla's advice on what dress to wear from her limited wardrobe.
c7:p19: Lucilla invites Mrs Chiley to be her chaperone at her father's dinner party that evening. c7:p20: Lucilla visits Mrs Chiley to invite her to be chaperone at Dr Marjoribanks's dinner party that evening. c7:p21: Lucilla visits Mrs. Chiley to invite her as a chaperone to Dr. Marjoribanks's dinner party that evening. When Mrs. Chiley anxiously asks what to wear, Lucilla advises her that it doesn't matter since only gentlemen will be present, and explains her principle of dressing only when ladies are attending—in simple white frocks worn high in the neck, as anything else would be bad style.
c7:p22: After Lucilla invites Mrs Chiley to chaperone her father's dinner party that evening, she visits the elderly widow at her home. c7:p23: Mrs Chiley is impressed by Lucilla's principle of never dressing for gentlemen, viewing it as extraordinary virtue. c7:p24: After successfully securing Mrs Chiley as a chaperone for the evening's dinner party, Lucilla returns home in a state of satisfied confidence, pleased with her manipulation of social conventions and her own superior judgment.
c7:p25: Lucilla returns from inviting Mrs. Chiley to the dinner party and consulting with Mr. Holden the upholsterer about new curtains. c7:p26: Miss Marjoribanks encounters a beggar woman with six children on Grange Lane. c7:p27: This chunk appears in paragraph P27, immediately after Lucilla's encounter with a beggar woman on Grange Lane. c7:p28: After inviting Mrs. Chiley to be her chaperone for the evening's dinner party, Lucilla visits the upholsterer Mr. Holden to select fabrics for renovating her father's house, examining a green damask in his shop mirrors.
c7:p29: Lucilla visits Mr. Holden's upholstery shop to select fabric for her home renovations. She examines a green damask fabric by holding it up to a mirror to test its color effect, then departs, leaving the upholsterer uncertain whether she intends to use the material for curtains or dresses.
c7:p30: Lucilla has just visited Mr. Holden's upholstery shop to select damask for new curtains. c7:p31: Lucilla is deciding whether to visit Barbara to invite her to sing at her father's dinner party that evening. c7:p32: Lucilla is deliberating whether to invite her friend Barbara to either perform at her father's dinner party that evening or to bring her to luncheon to entertain her cousin Tom, ultimately deciding against both options to avoid revealing her full capabilities too early and to protect Tom from unnecessary complications.
c7:p33: Lucilla deliberates whether to invite her friend Barbara to lunch to entertain her cousin Tom, but decides against it, fearing that other people might see Barbara and spoil her own plans to introduce her to society later as a grand success.

c7:p35: Lucilla has dismissed her cousin Tom from the morning, instructing him to return at half-past one only if he brings someone very amusing. c7:p39: Tom Marjoribanks brings an uninviting guest to lunch whom Lucilla had commissioned as "somebody amusing." This guest makes irreverent comments about a pending execution of a man who killed a tailor, treating it as entertainment for the provincial town, which shocks Miss Bury who is present.
c7:p40: The "amusing man" brought by Tom to lunch makes cynical remarks about an upcoming execution in Carlingford, treating a murder case as entertainment for a provincial town. c7:p41: Miss Bury, the Rector's sister, is visiting Lucilla when Tom arrives with a young barrister whom Lucilla had asked him to bring to lunch. c7:p43: The young barrister, brought by Tom as his "amusing" guest for luncheon, defends his callous remarks about a murderer awaiting execution by claiming that criminals of such a description lack souls entirely, arguing this is a fundamental distinction between different classes of mankind.
c7:p44: Miss Bury, the Rector's sister, is defending the souls of condemned criminals against a cynical young barrister's claim that murderers have no souls. c7:p45: Miss Bury, a devout woman visiting Lucilla, becomes distressed during lunch when Tom brings an irreverent young barrister who callously discusses an upcoming execution and claims that criminals have no souls. c7:p47: Miss Bury, a visiting clergyman's sister concerned with spiritual matters, challenges Tom after he uses the exclamation "By Jove!" during a heated discussion about a condemned murderer's soul. c7:p48: Tom has brought an amusing companion to luncheon at Lucilla's invitation. c7:p49: Lucilla receives an unwelcome visitor—Tom brings an "amusing" man to lunch as instructed, but this guest makes offensive remarks about a murderer lacking a soul. c7:p50: Lucilla is defending her religious orthodoxy and moral principles after Tom has brought an irreverent barrister to lunch who cynically dismissed the souls of criminals. c7:p51: Lucilla responds to a heated religious debate at luncheon, where a young barrister has offended Miss Bury by claiming that murderers have no souls. c7:p52: Lucilla diplomatically ends an awkward lunch with Miss Bury after Tom brings a cynical barrister who makes offensive remarks about the souls of criminals and uses profane language. c7:p53: After the "amusing man" Tom brought to lunch makes shockingly irreligious remarks about a condemned murderer's soul, Lucilla skillfully defuses the crisis by rebuking both men and asserting her orthodox principles. c7:p54: Miss Bury, the Rector's sister, has just witnessed an offensive lunch conversation where Tom's guest—a young barrister—made irreverent remarks about a murderer awaiting execution and blasphemously claimed certain people have no souls. c7:p55: After lunch with Tom and his unsuitable companion, Miss Bury accompanies Lucilla upstairs to the drawing room, troubled by the young men's irreligious remarks. c7:p56: Miss Bury has just witnessed an uncomfortable luncheon where Tom brought an unsuitable companion who made offensive remarks about a criminal case and denied that murderers have souls. Disturbed by this worldly and irreligious conversation, Miss Bury expresses concern about Lucilla's exposure to such corrupting influences and offers to recommend a respectable Christian woman as a companion to provide proper supervision.
c7:p57: Lucilla smoothly recovers from an awkward social disaster at luncheon, where Tom brings an amusing but irreverent barrister whose cynical remarks about a criminal case offend Miss Bury's religious sensibilities. c7:p58: Miss Bury has just warned Lucilla about the impropriety of receiving young men alone and offered to recommend a respectable Christian companion. c7:p59: Miss Bury, the Rector's sister, is departing after lunch and offers moral guidance to Lucilla about the importance of being careful with one's words, reflecting her concern about Lucilla's spiritual development and the inappropriate company of young men she has just witnessed at the luncheon table.
c7:p60: Lucilla reassures Miss Bury, the Rector's sister, that she shares her religious principles after an awkward luncheon where Tom brought an irreverent barrister who made offensive remarks about criminals lacking souls. c7:p61: Lucilla has successfully navigated a social crisis at luncheon when Tom brought an irreverent companion who offended Miss Bury with blasphemous remarks. c7:p62: After a failed lunch with Tom and an unsuitable guest who offended Miss Bury's religious sensibilities, Lucilla recovers her composure.
